lesson.title: Packing: How Multiple Values Become One Tuple
lesson.summary: Whenever you write comma-separated values without enclosing them in a list, Python quietly bundles them into a tuple, the same packing that makes multiple return values and multiple assignment possible.
lesson.body:
Packing is the name for the exact behavior you already saw in passing while learning Tuple Creation: when Python encounters a comma-separated sequence of values being assigned to a single name, it gathers, or "packs," all of those values into one tuple object before the assignment happens. The parentheses you often see around a tuple are optional decoration; the packing itself is triggered by the commas.

student = "Maya", 16, "10th grade"
print(student)
print(type(student))

This prints ('Maya', 16, '10th grade') and then <class 'tuple'>. Three separate values, a string, an integer, and another string, were packed into a single tuple object and bound to the one name student.

This is precisely the mechanism behind Multiple Return Values. When a function contains return a, b, Python packs a and b into a tuple at that exact moment, before the value ever leaves the function. The function is not doing anything exotic; it is just returning a value, and that value happens to be freshly packed. Packing also shows up any time you write something like point = 3, 4 without parentheses at all: Python still recognizes the comma and still produces a tuple.

Packing only does half the job, though. Having all your values bundled into one tuple is useful for passing them around together, but sooner or later you want them back out as separate names again. That reverse process, called unpacking, is the next concept, and it depends directly on tuples being packed this way in the first place.
